words.definition: going as planned, so that you will finish on time.
examples: The migration is on track for Friday.
We were behind last week, but we're back on track now.
words.mission: Say which of your tasks is on track today.

words.definition: help with a task, usually for a short time; used with give or need.
examples: Could someone give me a hand with the test data?
If you need a hand with the release, I'm free after lunch.
words.mission: Ask a colleague for a hand with one small task.

words.definition: to find the answer to a problem, or the reason for it, by thinking about it.
examples: I'm still trying to figure out why the import is slow.
We finally figured out how to reproduce it.
words.mission: Name one thing you are still figuring out, in today's stand-up.

words.definition: how fast something moves forward, compared with how fast it needs to go.
examples: We'll finish the migration on Thursday at this pace.
We need to pick up the pace if we want Friday.
words.mission: Say at what pace your main task is moving, and why.

words.definition: a short early warning that something is coming, so people are not surprised.
examples: Just a quick heads-up: the demo moves to Thursday.
Thanks for the heads-up, I'll plan the deploy around it.
words.mission: Give the team a heads-up about one change coming this week.

words.definition: not needed or used right now, so it is free for something else.
examples: Have you got a spare ten minutes this afternoon?
I'll use any spare time on Friday to tidy the tests.
words.mission: Say when you have a spare half hour this week.

words.trap: Not 'délai' (the time allowed, a deadline) — for that say deadline or lead time. A delay means something happens later than planned.
words.definition: the extra time you have to wait because something happens later than planned.
examples: There's a two-day delay on the export feature.
Sorry for the delay — the review took longer than expected.
words.mission: Announce a delay in one calm sentence: what, how long, why.

words.definition: from the very beginning, without using anything that was done before.
examples: I'm rewriting the import script from scratch.
It was faster to start from scratch than to fix the old one.
words.mission: Say what you would rather rebuild from scratch, and why.

words.definition: to do the work you are behind on, until you reach the point where you should be.
examples: I'll catch up on reviews this afternoon.
We lost a day on Monday but caught up by Thursday.
words.mission: Say what you will catch up on before Monday.

words.definition: an experience that is very difficult or unpleasant; used informally about work that went badly.

words.mission: Tell a colleague which part of your week was a nightmare.

words.mission: Start your update with 'so far' and what is done.

words.trap: Not 'bloqué' (blocked) for everything: say stuck on when the problem is the work itself; blocked when you are waiting for someone.
words.definition: not able to make progress with a problem, because you cannot find a way forward.

She was stuck on the same error for most of yesterday.
words.mission: Say what you are stuck on, then ask for ideas.

words.definition: a friendly, quick way to ask whether something you tried has worked yet.

Any luck finding the cause, or should I join you?

words.trap: Not 'je suis absent' → 'I'm absent' (that sounds like a school register): say I'm off tomorrow. Here off means not at work, not switched off.

words.mission: Tell the team when you are next off, and who covers.

words.definition: to look at or explain something carefully from beginning to end.
examples: Can we go through the plan once more before I start?
She went through the checklist with the new hire.
words.mission: Ask to go through one plan with someone today.

words.trap: Not the religious 'Assomption': in English it is any belief you have not checked.

words.mission: State one assumption out loud before you act on it.

words.definition: to check something a second time to be sure it is right.

words.mission: Double-check one thing before you send it, and say you did.

words.definition: to be clear and easy to understand; also used to check that someone has understood you.

words.definition: to reduce a large number of possibilities to a few, so a choice becomes easier.

words.mission: Narrow one vague request down to two concrete options.

words.mission: Ask for a rough idea instead of an exact figure today.

words.trap: Not 'éventuellement' (maybe, possibly) — for that say possibly or if needed. Eventually means in the end.

words.definition: useful and easy to use, especially in a practical way.

This script comes in handy every release.

words.definition: in simple, clear words that anyone can understand, without technical language.

words.definition: to wait and not do something yet, until you have more information.

words.definition: to tell someone a fact they may not have noticed, without blaming them.

words.definition: a polite way to say what you prefer to do instead.

words.definition: to be more important or bigger than something else, so it wins the decision.

words.trap: Say /ˈɔː.kwəd/ — the 'w' is silent.

words.definition: said to accept what someone says as reasonable, even if you had a different view.

words.definition: to start talking about a subject, especially one that is not easy.

words.mission: Soften one honest remark with 'no offence, but…'.

words.definition: used when you change your mind after thinking again.

words.mission: Change your mind out loud once with 'on second thought…'.

words.definition: to say something that is reasonable and worth listening to.

words.mission: Tell someone 'you have a point' when they do.

words.trap: Not 'pas de souci' translated as 'no problem' every time: no worries is the friendlier, everyday one.
words.definition: a friendly way to say that something is not a problem, or to accept an apology.
examples: No worries, I'll pick it up on Monday.

words.mission: Answer one apology with 'no worries' instead of 'it's nothing'.

words.definition: a temporary way to avoid a problem instead of fixing its cause.

words.mission: Name one workaround in your code that should become a fix.

words.definition: to find something or someone after searching in many places.

words.mission: Ask 'what's the root cause?' once about a bug today.

words.definition: not reliable; working sometimes and failing other times for no clear reason.
examples: That test is flaky — it fails one run in five.
The Wi-Fi in the meeting room is flaky.
words.mission: Call one unreliable thing 'flaky' and say how often it fails.

words.definition: to return a system to an earlier version because the new one causes problems.

words.trap: Not 'panne' translated as 'breakdown': for a service, say outage.

words.mission: Describe the last outage you saw in one sentence.

words.trap: Not 'sensible' in French (sensitive, easily hurt) — for that say sensitive. Sensible means reasonable.

examples: The sensible fix is to add a timeout.

words.mission: Call one option 'the sensible thing to do' and explain why.

words.definition: to decide that something is not possible or not the cause, so you stop considering it.

words.mission: Rule out one possible cause out loud, with your evidence.

words.definition: something annoying that takes time and effort, without being difficult.
examples: Rotating the keys is a hassle, but it's ten minutes.
Sorry for the hassle — the link works now.
words.mission: Apologise for one small hassle you caused, in one line.

words.definition: for now, until something changes.
examples: For the time being, use the old endpoint.
The workaround stays in place for the time being.
collocations: at least for the time being
words.mission: Say what stays as it is for the time being.

words.trap: Informal: fine in chat and with colleagues, not in an email to a client.
words.definition: an informal way to say that something was your mistake.
examples: My bad — I pushed to the wrong branch.
That typo was my bad, fixed now.
words.mission: Own one small mistake with 'my bad' instead of a long apology.

words.definition: when you look back at something after it has happened, and understand it better.
examples: In hindsight, we should have tested the rollback.
In hindsight the warning in the logs was obvious.
words.mission: Say one thing that is obvious in hindsight about a recent bug.

words.definition: working normally again after being stopped or set up.
examples: Good news: the API is up and running again.
The new laptop was up and running in an hour.
words.mission: Announce one thing that is back up and running.

words.definition: a small, sudden problem that stops something working properly for a short time.
examples: It was just a glitch — refresh and it's gone.
A rendering glitch hid the button on mobile.
words.mission: Call one small, short problem a glitch — not a bug.

words.definition: to move unfinished work from one period, such as a sprint, to the next.
examples: Two tickets will carry over to next sprint.
We carried over the export work again — third time.
words.mission: Say which task will carry over, and why, before anyone asks.

words.definition: extra freedom or time that lets you change a plan without breaking it.
examples: We have some leeway on the date, but not on the budget.
Give the estimate a bit of leeway for surprises.
words.mission: Say where your plan has leeway and where it has none.

words.definition: approximate; used for a number that gives an idea but is not exact.
examples: Give me a ballpark figure — a week or a month?
The ballpark cost is around ten days of work.
words.mission: Ask for a ballpark figure instead of an exact estimate.

words.definition: to divide something big into smaller parts so it is easier to plan or understand.
examples: Let's break the epic down into tickets we can estimate.
She broke the cost down by team.
words.mission: Break one big task down into three smaller ones, out loud.

words.definition: to do something faster or cheaper by skipping steps, so the quality suffers.
examples: If we cut corners on tests now, we pay for it in June.
The vendor clearly cut corners on the security review.
words.mission: Name one place where the plan cuts corners, and the cost of it.

words.trap: Not only the memory buffer: in planning it means spare time you keep for surprises.
words.definition: extra time or resources added to a plan to absorb surprises.
examples: I added a two-day buffer before the demo.
Without a buffer, one sick day breaks the plan.
words.mission: Say how much buffer your estimate includes.

words.trap: Not 'tentative' in French (an attempt) — for that say attempt. Tentative means not final yet.
words.definition: not final or certain; likely to change.
examples: The date is tentative — don't tell the client yet.

words.mission: Mark one date as tentative when you share it.

words.definition: to approve something officially so that work can go ahead.
examples: Who needs to sign off on the scope before we start?
Legal signed off on the wording yesterday.
words.mission: Ask who has to sign off on your plan, and by when.

words.definition: to stop working for now, because enough has been done or you are tired.
examples: It's six o'clock — let's call it a day.
We called it a day after the third failed deploy.
words.mission: Say 'let's call it a day' at the end of one long session.

examples: Five features in one sprint is a stretch.

words.mission: Call one target 'a stretch' and say what would make it realistic.

words.definition: informed about what is happening, and included in the messages about it.
examples: Keep me in the loop on the vendor talks.

words.mission: Ask to be kept in the loop on one topic.

words.definition: said after a number to mean it could be a little more or a little less.

Two hundred users, give or take a few.
words.mission: Add 'give or take' to one estimate today.

words.definition: an attempt that will probably not succeed but is worth trying.

words.mission: Call one idea a long shot, then try it anyway.

words.definition: having far too much work to deal with.
examples: I'm swamped this week — can it wait?
Support is swamped after the release.
words.mission: Tell someone you are swamped instead of saying nothing.

words.definition: to fail to notice something, usually a small but important detail.

Easy to overlook, but the index is never dropped.
words.mission: Say 'I overlooked …' instead of 'I didn't see' once today.

words.definition: to check something carefully, part by part, before you accept it.

words.mission: Ask someone to go over one piece of your work.

words.definition: done carelessly, without enough attention to detail.
examples: The error handling is a bit sloppy here.

words.mission: Describe one thing as 'a bit sloppy' — the work, never the person.

words.definition: to make something neater by removing what is unnecessary or messy.
examples: I'll tidy up the imports before merging.
She tidied up the tests so they read top to bottom.
words.mission: Tidy up one small thing in a file you touch today.

words.definition: remaining after the rest has been used, removed or finished.
examples: There's some leftover code from the old flow.

words.mission: Find one leftover thing in the codebase and name it.

words.definition: to criticise very small details that do not really matter.

words.mission: Label one small comment 'nitpick:' so nobody treats it as a blocker.

words.definition: said to thank someone who noticed a mistake or a risk before it caused harm.

words.mission: Say 'good catch' to the next person who finds your mistake.

words.definition: not able to decide between two options.

words.mission: Say what you are on the fence about, and what would decide it.

words.definition: a situation or thing that is untidy, confused or badly organised.

words.mission: Call one thing a mess and offer to clean it up.

words.definition: to gently remind or push someone to do something.

words.mission: Nudge one person about one thing, politely.

words.definition: when you look at something quickly for the first time, before checking properly.

words.mission: Start one review comment with 'at first glance …'.

words.definition: to contact someone, especially to offer or ask for help.

words.mission: Reach out to one person you have been meaning to contact.
